description_full: The Middleby Corporation operates in the foodservice industry worldwide. The company develops and manufactures a line of solutions used in commercial foodservice and food processing. It offers conveyor, combi, convection, baking, proofing, deck, speed cooking, and hydrovection ovens; ranges, fryers, and rethermalizers; steam cooking, food warming, catering, induction, and countertop cooking equipment; heated cabinets, charbroilers, ventless cooking systems, kitchen ventilation, toasters, griddles, charcoal grills, professional mixers and refrigerators, stainless steel fabrication, custom millwork, blast chillers, coldrooms, ice machines, and frozen dessert equipment; soft serve ice cream, coffee and beverage dispensing, home and professional craft brewing equipment; and fry dispenser, bottle filling and canning equipment, IoT solutions, and controls development and manufacturing. The company was formerly known as Middleby Marshall Oven Company and changed its name to The Middleby Corporation in 1985. The Middleby Corporation was founded in 1888 and is based in Elgin, Illinois.

financial_summary: The Middleby Corporation is a mid-cap industrials business with a $6.2B market cap on $3.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -7% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 9% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, with gross margins sitting at 39%.
The business throws off $559M in free cash flow — roughly 17 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.
Accruals are elevated at -14.4% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.9× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.1×.

Management returns a meaningful 11.7% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 10% over the past year excluding the latest month.

val: The stock trades 25% below its DCF fair value of $183, a meaningful margin of safety.

Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 9.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 9 covering analysts target $155 on average, 13% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 9% earns above the cost of capital of 8.4%, but the 1pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.23).

Earnings quality is a concern: a weak Piotroski score of 3/9, cash conversion of only -2.27x and high accruals (-14.4% of assets).

hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.9x net debt to EBITDA ($222.2M of cash against $2.2B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.1x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.1, in the safe zone).

growth: Revenue has compounded at -7.4% over 3 years, 5.0% over 5 years and 5.8% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 15%).
At current returns, reinvesting 32% of profits supports about 2.9% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 2.7% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (2.2% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 22, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.7%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 11.7% a year to shareholders (11.7% in buybacks).
people: With about 8,826 employees, each generates about $363K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 10.5% a year.
That works out to $63K of free cash flow per employee.
Compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
